title: Two tax systems on one income
teaches: How the US and Portugal share the tax on an American living in Portugal, what happens to each kind of US account, and the paperwork that comes with money in two countries

blocks.text: An American who moves to Lisbon keeps filing a US return every year, on the same brackets as before, for as long as they hold a US passport. Portugal now taxes them too, on the same income. Left alone, the two taxes would simply add up.

They don't add up, because of two pieces of machinery: the tax treaty between the two countries, signed in 1994, and the US foreign tax credit. Between them, a US citizen in Portugal ends up paying roughly the larger of the two countries' bills rather than both. Lesson P1 showed that Portugal's bill on pension income is usually the larger one by a wide margin, so in practice the American living in Portugal pays about Portugal's tax, and the US return mostly records that nothing more is owed.

The treaty does less for a citizen than for anyone else. Like every US treaty, it contains a saving clause that keeps the US's right to tax its own citizens as if the treaty didn't exist, with a few exceptions.[^saving] Most of the relief therefore runs through credits rather than exemptions.

For each kind of income, the treaty names a country that has the first claim and a country that gives a credit. Portugal, as the country of residence, taxes everything. The US taxes its citizen on everything too. Where Portugal's tax is higher, the US credit for it wipes out the US tax; where the US tax is higher, the American pays the difference to the US.

**Private pensions and IRA withdrawals.** Under the treaty these are taxed by the country of residence, so Portugal applies its progressive rates. The US taxes them as well, and credits Portugal's tax against its own.[^resource]

**Social Security.** The treaty lets the US tax it. Portugal's tax authority reads that as permission rather than exclusion and taxes it as a pension too; some advisers argue the opposite, and the question has gone both ways in practice.[^ss] This course takes the cautious reading.

**Dividends and gains.** Portugal taxes them at its flat 28 percent. The US taxes them at 0, 15 or 20 percent. So a retiree who planned to live off gains in the US 0 percent band, lesson 7's best case, finds Portugal charging 28 percent on every dollar of gain.

**Wages.** An American working in Portugal can exclude up to $132,900 of foreign earnings from US tax in 2026, or credit the Portuguese tax instead. The exclusion applies only to pay for work, never to pensions, IRA withdrawals or investment income.

The figure is a rough model of one couple's year. Portugal's tax is worked out as in P1, with Social Security counted as a pension and gains at 28 percent, and the bill in Portugal is taken as the larger of the two countries' taxes.

blocks.caption: A couple's federal tax living in Washington, against their tax living in Portugal, with withdrawals from IRAs, gains and dividends, and Social Security set by the sliders.
blocks.task: Raise the gains and dividends to $80,000 or more

blocks.text: With $40,000 from IRAs and $40,000 of gains, the couple pays $780 of federal tax in Washington and about $15,200 in Portugal, nearly all of it the 28 percent on gains. A couple living entirely on $80,000 of gains pays nothing to the US and $22,400 to Portugal. Adding $40,000 of Social Security to the first couple takes them from $4,520 in Washington to about $25,800 in Portugal.

parts.title: Each US account, seen from Portugal

blocks.text: Lesson 8 compared the four buckets by the tax rate going in and the rate coming out. In Portugal the rate going in is history, and the rate coming out is Portugal's.

**Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s** are taxed as pensions when withdrawn, at the progressive rates. A large pre-tax balance withdrawn over a Portuguese retirement meets Portugal's 35 to 48 percent brackets instead of the US 12 or 22.

**Roth IRAs** are the open question. Portugal has no Roth, and nothing in its law or the treaty says withdrawals are tax-free. Some advisers treat the original contributions as returned capital and tax only the growth; some treat the whole account as a pension. Until Portugal's tax authority or a court rules, a Roth is safest planned as taxable in Portugal on its growth, at either the progressive rates or 28 percent.
**HSAs** aren't recognised at all. Portugal sees an ordinary investment account, so the growth can be taxed as it happens or on withdrawal, even when the money pays for medical care.

**Taxable brokerage accounts** have their gains taxed at 28 percent, measured in euros: the cost in euros at the date of purchase against the price in euros at sale. A share bought for $100 when the dollar bought 0.95 euro and sold for $100 when it bought 0.87 has made no gain in dollars and a loss in euros; the reverse move makes a gain out of nothing. Portugal gives no step-up on arrival, so gains built up before the move are taxed when realised there.
Because Portugal's rates are higher on nearly everything a retiree owns, the years before the move are the cheap ones, and three of the trunk's ideas become more urgent.

**Harvest gains at 0 percent.** Selling and rebuying shares within the US 0 percent band, lesson 10's gain harvesting, raises the basis. Each dollar of basis raised is a dollar Portugal can't tax at 28 percent later.

**Convert to Roth at US rates.** A conversion taxed at 12 or 22 percent in the US, before residence in Portugal begins, empties pre-tax money that Portugal would otherwise tax at its progressive rates. That still leaves the Roth's own treatment uncertain, so this works best when the Roth is spent mostly on its basis.
**Time the move.** Residence usually begins on arrival, with the year split. Large gains or conversions belong in the US part of that year, or the year before.
Money in two countries brings forms in both.

**In the US.** An FBAR lists every foreign account whenever their combined value passed $10,000 at any point in the year, including a Portuguese current account. Form 8938 overlaps it for larger sums: for a couple living abroad, above $400,000 at year end or $600,000 at any time. The penalties for missing either are severe, and both are easy to file.
**In Portugal.** The annual return lists foreign income on its own annex, and the bank, the broker and each US account must be declared.

**Funds.** A Portuguese or other European fund held by a US citizen is a PFIC under US law, taxed so harshly that it is almost always a mistake.[^pfic] And an EU broker usually won't sell a US-listed fund to an EU resident, because the fund lacks the short disclosure document EU rules require.[^priips] So Americans in Portugal mostly keep their US brokerage accounts, but not every US broker will keep a client with a foreign address. Some do; finding one before the move saves a forced sale later.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A US citizen in Portugal files in both countries and pays roughly the larger of the two taxes, after the treaty and the foreign tax credit.
Portugal taxes IRA withdrawals as pensions, Social Security too on its reading, and gains at a flat 28 percent measured in euros.
The Roth's treatment in Portugal is unsettled, and the HSA isn't recognised.
Gain harvesting and Roth conversions at US rates are worth most in the years before moving.
Foreign accounts above $10,000 need an FBAR, and European funds are PFICs: keep a US broker that accepts foreign addresses.

blocks.caption: Five questions on two tax systems
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: An American couple moves to Portugal. Roughly what do they pay in tax on their pensions?
choices: About the larger of the two countries' taxes
The two countries' taxes added together
Only the US tax, because of the treaty
items.why: The treaty and the foreign tax credit stop the two bills adding up, and for most retirees Portugal's is the larger.

items.ask: Can the foreign earned income exclusion shelter an American's IRA withdrawals from US tax while they live in Portugal?
choices: No, it applies only to pay for work
Yes, but only for Roth accounts
items.why: The exclusion covers foreign earned income. Pensions, withdrawals and investment income are never earned income.

items.ask: Why does a retiree who lives on gains lose most by moving to Portugal?
choices: Portugal taxes gains at 28 percent, where the US band can be 0
Portugal doesn't allow selling US shares
The US doubles its rate on gains for citizens abroad
items.why: The US 0 percent band for gains has no Portuguese equivalent.

items.ask: Which step before moving reduces what Portugal can later tax on a brokerage account?
choices: Harvesting gains at the US 0 percent rate to raise the basis
Moving the account to a Portuguese bank
Converting the shares to an HSA
items.why: Portugal taxes the gain above the cost, so a higher basis set while in the US leaves less gain to tax at 28 percent.

items.ask: Why do most Americans in Portugal keep a US brokerage account?
choices: European funds are PFICs for them, and EU brokers rarely sell US funds
Portugal forbids foreigners from opening accounts
US accounts are exempt from Portuguese tax
items.why: Each side's rules block the other's funds, so a US broker that accepts foreign addresses is usually the way through.

summary: **Citizens are taxed wherever they live.** The US return goes on after the move, alongside Portugal's.
**The two taxes don't add up.** The treaty and the foreign tax credit leave roughly the larger of the two to pay.
**Portugal's is usually the larger.** IRA withdrawals meet its progressive rates and gains a flat 28 percent.
**Social Security is taxed in Portugal on its reading.** The treaty is read both ways, so plan for the cautious one.
**The Roth and the HSA travel badly.** The Roth's treatment is unsettled and the HSA isn't recognised.
**The cheap years come before the move.** Harvest gains and convert to Roth at US rates while still resident in the US.
**File the FBAR and avoid European funds.** Keep a US broker that serves clients living abroad.

saving.title: The saving clause
saving.text: Article 1 of the treaty lets the US tax its citizens and residents as if the treaty had not come into effect. The exceptions it lists include the relief from double taxation article, which is the one that matters here, and some pension and social security rules.

resource.title: Re-sourcing
resource.text: The US credit is normally limited to foreign tax on foreign income, and an IRA withdrawal is US income. The treaty's double taxation article re-sources income so that the US credits Portugal's tax on it anyway, after Portugal first credits whatever tax the US could charge a non-citizen. The order is fiddly; the effect is close to paying the larger of the two.

ss.title: The Social Security dispute
ss.text: Article 20 of the treaty says US social security benefits paid to a Portuguese resident may be taxed in the US. The word 'may' leaves Portugal free to tax them too, which is how Portugal's tax authority reads it. Other treaties word the same rule as 'shall be taxable only', and the difference is the whole dispute.

pfic.title: PFICs
pfic.text: A passive foreign investment company is, broadly, any non-US fund. Unless the owner makes an election that the fund rarely supports, gains are taxed at the highest US rate with an interest charge, and an annual Form 8621 is due for each fund.

priips.title: Why EU brokers won't sell US funds
priips.text: EU rules on packaged retail investments require a short summary sheet, the KID, in the investor's language. US fund companies don't produce one, so EU brokers refuse retail orders for US-listed funds. Single shares and some professional-client arrangements are outside the rule.
